items.readable_text:
Content:
When seeking an approximate solution to a nonlinear system of equations, the first thing we should do is sketch a graph of the system and get a visual approximation for the intersection point.

Content:
For example, suppose we wish to seek an approximate solution to the following system of equations:

Content:
[MATH: {y = (1)/(2)x + 1; y = 2^{4 − x}]

Content:
The solution of this system corresponds to the point of intersection of the two curves shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a8ce32a0f8437d52273bc281ebe1eff5]

Content:
The diagram suggests that [MATH: x\approx 2.7] and [MATH: y\approx 2.4] is an approximate solution.

Content:
At this stage, we're simply making a visual estimate based on the graph. We don't know if [MATH: x] is closer to [MATH: 2.7] or [MATH: 2.8,] for example. We'll learn how to improve our estimate later in this lesson.

Content:
Let's return to the following system of equations:

Content:
[MATH: {y = (1)/(2)x + 1; y = 2^{4 − x}]

Content:
As we saw, the solution of this system corresponds to the intersection of the two curves shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a5e1cf00c8ff96dbbd16db00e5ec86d]

Content:
Earlier, we gave [MATH: x\approx 2.7] as an approximate solution, but this was a rough guess. We now wish to improve on this solution.

Content:
If we look again, the diagram suggests that the [MATH: x]-value at the intersection point lies somewhere between [MATH: 2.5] and [MATH: 3.] So, some good candidates for our approximate solution (to one decimal place) are

Content:
[MATH: 2.6, \qquad 2.7, \qquad 2.8, \qquad 2.9, \qquad 3.0.]

Content:
To see which of these give the best solution, we define the functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] as
[MATH: f(x)=\dfrac12x + 1, \qquad g(x)=2^{4-x}.]

Content:
The [MATH: x]-coordinate of the intersection point corresponds to the solution of

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=g(x)]

Content:
which is equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: f(x) - g(x) = 0.]

Content:
Next, we create a table of values, as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2.6] | [MATH: 2.7] | [MATH: 2.8] | [MATH: 2.9] | [MATH: 3.0] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | | | | | |
| [MATH: g(x)] | | | | | |

Content:
To determine which of our candidates gives the best approximation to our system, we compute the error for each candidate, given by [MATH: |f(x)-g(x)|.] Since our system is equivalent to [MATH: f(x) - g(x) = 0,] the error should be small near the intersection point.

Content:
Filling in our table of values, we get the following:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2.6] | [MATH: 2.7] | [MATH: 2.8] | [MATH: 2.9] | [MATH: 3.0] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: 2.30] | [MATH: 2.35] | [MATH: 2.40] | [MATH: 2.45] | [MATH: 2.50] |
| [MATH: g(x)] | [MATH: 2.64] | [MATH: 2.46] | [MATH: 2.30] | [MATH: 2.14] | [MATH: 2.00] |
| [MATH: f(x)-g(x)] | [MATH: -0.34] | [MATH: -0.11] | [MATH: 0.10] | [MATH: 0.31] | [MATH: 0.50] |
| [MATH: |f(x)-g(x)|] | [MATH: 0.34] | [MATH: 0.11] | [MATH: 0.10] | [MATH: 0.31] | [MATH: 0.50] |

Content:
The smallest error is [MATH: 0.10,] given by the value [MATH: x=2.8.]

Content:
Therefore, among the given options, the best approximation to the system is [MATH: x=2.8.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Many simple-looking equations cannot be solved using algebra. In such cases, we can only approximate the solution. Therefore, we need a test to determine whether a given solution is correct to an appropriate degree of accuracy. What test can we use for this?

Content:
For example, suppose we wish to solve [MATH: f(x) = g(x),] where the functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] are defined as

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = x^3, \qquad g(x) = 3^{-x}.]

Content:
Rounded to one decimal place, the solution is [MATH: x\approx 0.8.] To test this claim, we first consider the lower and upper bounds of [MATH: 0.8\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- the lower bound of [MATH: 0.8] is [MATH: 0.8 - 0.05 = 0.75,] and
- the upper bound of [MATH: 0.8] is [MATH: 0.8 + 0.05 = 0.85.]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: f(x) = g(x)] is equivalent to [MATH: f(x) - g(x) = 0.] So, to test that [MATH: x\approx 0.8] rounded to one decimal place, we compute [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] for both the upper and lower bound and look for a change in sign:

Content:
Computing [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] at the lower bound, we get
[MATH: f(0.75) − g(0.75)|= 0.75^{3} − 3^{− 0.75}; ≈ − 0.02]
which is negative.

Content:
Then, we compute [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] at the upper bound. We get
[MATH: f(0.85) − g(0.85)|= 0.85^{3} − 3^{− 0.85}; ≈ 0.22]
which is positive.

Content:
Since there is a change in sign, this confirms that the solution to the equation [MATH: f(x) = g(x)] is [MATH: x\approx 0.8,] rounded to one decimal place.

Content:
Finally, it can be shown that the "exact" solution to the equation is

Content:
[MATH: x =0.757\,696\,978\,830\,077\,\ldots\,.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When seeking an approximate solution to a nonlinear system of equations, the first thing we should do is sketch a graph of the system and get a visual approximation for the intersection point.

Content:
For example, suppose we wish to seek an approximate solution to the following system of equations:

Content:
[MATH: {y = (1)/(2)x + 1; y = 2^{4 − x}]

Content:
The solution of this system corresponds to the point of intersection of the two curves shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a8ce32a0f8437d52273bc281ebe1eff5]

Content:
The diagram suggests that [MATH: x\approx 2.7] and [MATH: y\approx 2.4] is an approximate solution.

Content:
At this stage, we're simply making a visual estimate based on the graph. We don't know if [MATH: x] is closer to [MATH: 2.7] or [MATH: 2.8,] for example. We'll learn how to improve our estimate later in this lesson.

---

Item 2 — Example: Approximating the Solution to a System of Nonlinear Equations Using a Graph

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/6fcba67f4e198758e6d14901593bb6f5]

Using the graph, find an approximate solution to the system of equations below.

[MATH: {y + x^{3} = 4; y = 2x^{2} − 1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The solution to the system of equations corresponds to the point of intersection of the two curves.

[IMG: /graphics/2c3a2ee27cd03b65db38572efe27c603]

From the graph, we see that [MATH: x \approx 1.2] and [MATH: y \approx 2.1] is an approximate solution.

---

Item 3 — Question 1

Question Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/q-45096]

Prompt:
Which of the following is an approximate solution to the system of equations below?
[MATH: {3x − y = 3; y = sqrt(x + 2)]

Choices:
a. [MATH: x ≈ 1.6] and [MATH: y ≈ − 2]
b. [MATH: x ≈ 1.6] and [MATH: y ≈ 1.9]
c. [MATH: x ≈ − 2] and [MATH: y ≈ − 2.5]
d. [MATH: x ≈ − 1.6] and [MATH: y ≈ 1.9]
e. [MATH: x ≈ 1.6] and [MATH: y ≈ 3.9]

---

Item 4 — Question 2

Question Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/q-45339]

Prompt:
Which of the following is an approximate solution to the system of equations below?
[MATH: {y = 2sqrt(x + 2); y = − 2sqrt(x) + 8]

Choices:
a. [MATH: x ≈ 3] and [MATH: y ≈ 4.5]
b. [MATH: x ≈ 2.6] and [MATH: y ≈ 0.5]
c. [MATH: x ≈ 0] and [MATH: y ≈ 6]
d. [MATH: x ≈ 3] and [MATH: y ≈ 6]
e. [MATH: x ≈ 0] and [MATH: y ≈ 4.5]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Improving an Approximate Solution

Content:
Let's return to the following system of equations:

Content:
[MATH: {y = (1)/(2)x + 1; y = 2^{4 − x}]

Content:
As we saw, the solution of this system corresponds to the intersection of the two curves shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a5e1cf00c8ff96dbbd16db00e5ec86d]

Content:
Earlier, we gave [MATH: x\approx 2.7] as an approximate solution, but this was a rough guess. We now wish to improve on this solution.

Content:
If we look again, the diagram suggests that the [MATH: x]-value at the intersection point lies somewhere between [MATH: 2.5] and [MATH: 3.] So, some good candidates for our approximate solution (to one decimal place) are

Content:
[MATH: 2.6, \qquad 2.7, \qquad 2.8, \qquad 2.9, \qquad 3.0.]

Content:
To see which of these give the best solution, we define the functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] as
[MATH: f(x)=\dfrac12x + 1, \qquad g(x)=2^{4-x}.]

Content:
The [MATH: x]-coordinate of the intersection point corresponds to the solution of

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=g(x)]

Content:
which is equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: f(x) - g(x) = 0.]

Content:
Next, we create a table of values, as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2.6] | [MATH: 2.7] | [MATH: 2.8] | [MATH: 2.9] | [MATH: 3.0] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | | | | | |
| [MATH: g(x)] | | | | | |
| [MATH: f(x)-g(x)] | | | | | |
| [MATH: |f(x)-g(x)|] | | | | | |

Content:
To determine which of our candidates gives the best approximation to our system, we compute the error for each candidate, given by [MATH: |f(x)-g(x)|.] Since our system is equivalent to [MATH: f(x) - g(x) = 0,] the error should be small near the intersection point.

Content:
Filling in our table of values, we get the following:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2.6] | [MATH: 2.7] | [MATH: 2.8] | [MATH: 2.9] | [MATH: 3.0] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: 2.30] | [MATH: 2.35] | [MATH: 2.40] | [MATH: 2.45] | [MATH: 2.50] |
| [MATH: g(x)] | [MATH: 2.64] | [MATH: 2.46] | [MATH: 2.30] | [MATH: 2.14] | [MATH: 2.00] |
| [MATH: f(x)-g(x)] | [MATH: -0.34] | [MATH: -0.11] | [MATH: 0.10] | [MATH: 0.31] | [MATH: 0.50] |
| [MATH: |f(x)-g(x)|] | [MATH: 0.34] | [MATH: 0.11] | [MATH: 0.10] | [MATH: 0.31] | [MATH: 0.50] |

Content:
The smallest error is [MATH: 0.10,] given by the value [MATH: x=2.8.]

Content:
Therefore, among the given options, the best approximation to the system is [MATH: x=2.8.]

---

| [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] | | [MATH: 0.33] | | | [MATH: -0.15] |

Explanation:
We fill in the table and get the following result:

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2.5] | [MATH: 2.6] | [MATH: 2.7] | [MATH: 2.8] | [MATH: 2.9] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: 5.5] | [MATH: 5.4] | [MATH: 5.3] | [MATH: 5.2] | [MATH: 5.1] |
| [MATH: g(x)] | [MATH: 5.00] | [MATH: 5.07] | [MATH: 5.13] | [MATH: 5.19] | [MATH: 5.25] |
| [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] | [MATH: 0.50] | [MATH: 0.33] | [MATH: 0.17] | [MATH: 0.01] | [MATH: -0.15] |
| [MATH: |f(x)-g(x)|] | [MATH: 0.50] | [MATH: 0.33] | [MATH: 0.17] | [MATH: 0.01] | [MATH: 0.15] |

The expression [MATH: |f(x)-g(x)|] gives the error. The smallest error is [MATH: 0.01,] given by the value [MATH: x=2.8.]

Therefore, among the given options, the best approximation to the solution is [MATH: x=2.8.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Using Upper and Lower Bounds

Content:
Many simple-looking equations cannot be solved using algebra. In such cases, we can only approximate the solution. Therefore, we need a test to determine whether a given solution is correct to an appropriate degree of accuracy. What test can we use for this?

Content:
For example, suppose we wish to solve [MATH: f(x) = g(x),] where the functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] are defined as

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = x^3, \qquad g(x) = 3^{-x}.]

Content:
Rounded to one decimal place, the solution is [MATH: x\approx 0.8.] To test this claim, we first consider the lower and upper bounds of [MATH: 0.8\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- the lower bound of [MATH: 0.8] is [MATH: 0.8 - 0.05 = 0.75,] and
- the upper bound of [MATH: 0.8] is [MATH: 0.8 + 0.05 = 0.85.]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: f(x) = g(x)] is equivalent to [MATH: f(x) - g(x) = 0.] So, to test that [MATH: x\approx 0.8] rounded to one decimal place, we compute [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] for both the upper and lower bound and look for a change in sign:

Content:
Computing [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] at the lower bound, we get
[MATH: f(0.75) − g(0.75)|= 0.75^{3} − 3^{− 0.75}; ≈ − 0.02]
which is negative.

Content:
Then, we compute [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] at the upper bound. We get
[MATH: f(0.85) − g(0.85)|= 0.85^{3} − 3^{− 0.85}; ≈ 0.22]
which is positive.

Content:
Since there is a change in sign, this confirms that the solution to the equation [MATH: f(x) = g(x)] is [MATH: x\approx 0.8,] rounded to one decimal place.

Content:
Finally, it can be shown that the "exact" solution to the equation is

Content:
[MATH: x =0.757\,696\,978\,830\,077\,\ldots\,.]

From the graph, we identify that the point of intersection lies between [MATH: x=2.6] and [MATH: x=2.8.] So, we create a table of values as follows:

It appears from the table that the solution to [MATH: f(x) = g(x)] is [MATH: x \approx 2.7,] rounded to one decimal place.

We can verify that this the case by computing [MATH: f(x) - g(x)] for the upper and lower bounds of [MATH: x\approx 2.7] and checking for a change in sign:
[MATH: f(2.65) − g(2.65)|= (2.65 − 2) − (2(2.65))/((2.65)^{2} + 1); ≈ − 0.01 < 0; f(2.75) − g(2.75)|= (2.75 − 2) − (2(2.75))/((2.75)^{2} + 1); ≈ 0.11 > 0]
